other_side: NLW's answer to a model that makes familiar work no better, and sometimes worse, is that you should go looking for work you have never done: games, video pipelines, 3D, simulators. Zitron's Manifesto, written three weeks before Astra, reads that instruction as the tell. He says LLMs have got better in ways that are increasingly hard to define and that do not make economic sense for the user, that constant model churn makes it impossible to know whether the model improved or you merely got better at building harnesses round it, and that newer models often burn more tokens to do the same job, so the price of work rises while the price of intelligence falls. The call to experiment he treats, borrowing Robin Sloan's word, as "Jarvising": tinkering that feels like productivity and produces none, sustained by the fact that the only way to find out whether it works is to spend more money. His own experiments "sort of worked" after repeated prodding; the tolerable use, in his telling, is small, bounded, verifiable tasks, and the technology is "not useful enough to be profitable nor reliable enough to be world-changing".
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether the value of a new model shows up in work that already exists. Both accept as fact that Astra does not make ordinary tasks noticeably better: NLW says so in his opening, Zitron's whole essay is built on it. Both accept that serious coders have retreated to an older model on cost, and that benchmark gains no longer map onto felt usefulness. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the novel capabilities, games, video pipelines, 3D, interactive proposals, become paid, repeated, non-hobbyist work within a year. The observable is retention: how many of this month's weekend Astra experiments are still running, and being paid for, in a year. The worldview residue is whether tinkering is discovery or displacement activity. NLW is vindicated if a recognisable class of business output, the interactive proposal or the custom video pipeline, becomes routine; Zitron if the experiments stay demos and the bills keep rising. Both are polemicists with incentives, one bullish and anti-doom, the other bubble-certain and anti-hype; the signal is that both concede the efficiency story has stalled at the frontier. Watch whether Astra's coding revenue recovers or whether OpenAI quietly reprices it.
